::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Ocean phytoplankton emit dimethyl sulfide ($\text{DMS}$), whose oxidation products seed marine clouds and set the pre-industrial aerosol baseline. Models long missed a fast autoxidation route to hydroperoxymethyl thioformate ($\text{HPMTF}$); adding it to $\text{CESM2}$ sends about a third of marine sulfur through $\text{HPMTF}$, moves sulfate aloft and shifts anthropogenic aerosol forcing by $+0.11\text{ W m}^{-2}$. Afterwards you can explain why one intermediate changes a global forcing estimate.
:::

## The marine sulfur cycle and the CLAW hypothesis

In 1987, Charlson, Lovelock, Andreae, and Warren proposed the famous **CLAW Hypothesis**[^1]: oceanic phytoplankton produce dimethyl sulfide ($\text{CH}_3\text{SCH}_3$, or $\text{DMS}$), which ventilates into the atmosphere, oxidizes into sulfuric acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) and methanesulfonic acid ($\text{MSA}$), and forms **cloud condensation nuclei (CCN)**. These CCN brighten marine stratus clouds, increasing planetary albedo and cooling the surface:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Phyto["Marine Phytoplankton (DMSP)"] -->|Enzymatic Cleavage| DMS_Ocean["Oceanic DMS"]
    DMS_Ocean -->|Air-Sea Gas Transfer| DMS_Atm["Atmospheric DMS Gas"]
    DMS_Atm -->|OH / NO3 / Halogen Oxidation| SO2["SO2 + H2SO4 + MSA"]
    DMS_Atm -->|Isomerization Autoxidation| HPMTF["HPMTF Intermediate"]
    SO2 -->|New Particle Formation & Condensation| CCN["Marine Cloud Condensation Nuclei"]
    HPMTF -->|Cloud Droplet Scavenging| CloudSulfate["In-Cloud Aqueous Sulfate"]
    CCN -->|Aerosol Indirect Effect| CloudAlbedo["Brightened Marine Stratocumulus"]
    CloudAlbedo -->|Solar Reflection| Cooling["Surface Climate Cooling"]

    class Phyto olive
    class DMS_Atm indigo
    class HPMTF ochre
    class CloudAlbedo plum
    class Cooling sage
    classDef indigo fill:#1d4a62,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef plum fill:#48304a,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef olive fill:#5b6e34,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
    classDef ochre fill:#d69a2e,stroke:#3b1a18,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#3b1a18
    classDef sage fill:#95a87f,stroke:#3b1a18,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#3b1a18
```

Despite its foundational role, global Earth System Models have long struggled with high uncertainty in pristine oceanic aerosol indirect forcing. A primary reason was an incomplete chemical picture: classical models assumed $\text{DMS}$ oxidized solely via simple H-abstraction and OH-addition into $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{DMSO}$.

## Fast autoxidation to HPMTF

In 2019–2020, airborne mass spectrometry measurements during the NASA ATom campaign and laboratory chamber kinetics discovered a previously unrepresented intermediate: **hydroperoxymethyl thioformate** ($\text{HOOCH}_2\text{SCHO}$, or $\text{HPMTF}$)[^2].

When $\text{OH}$ abstracts a hydrogen atom from $\text{DMS}$, the resulting peroxy radical undergoes rapid intramolecular H-shift isomerization (autoxidation):

$$\text{CH}_3\text{SCH}_2\text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{intramolecular H-shift}} \cdot\text{CH}_2\text{SCH}_2\text{OOH} \xrightarrow{+\text{O}_2} \text{O}_2\text{CH}_2\text{SCH}_2\text{OOH} \xrightarrow{\text{fast decomposition}} \text{HOOCH}_2\text{SCHO} (\text{HPMTF}) + \text{OH}$$

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    DMS["DMS (CH3SCH3)"] -->|"OH addition"| DMSO["DMSO / DMSO2"]
    DMS -->|"OH or NO3 H-abstraction"| RO2["CH3SCH2OO peroxy radical"]
    DMSO --> MSA["MSA / SO2 / H2SO4"]
    RO2 -->|"traditional NO or HO2 route"| SO2["SO2 + formaldehyde"]
    RO2 -->|"intramolecular H-shift autoxidation"| HPMTF["HPMTF (HOOCH2SCHO)"]
    HPMTF -->|"gas-phase OH, cloud-free air"| OCS["OCS / SO2 lofted aloft"]
    HPMTF -->|"cloud droplet uptake"| AQ["in-cloud aqueous sulfate"]
    SO2 --> CCN["new particle formation, CCN"]
    MSA --> CCN

    class HPMTF rust
    style AQ stroke:#1E88E5,stroke-width:3px
    style OCS stroke:#1E88E5,stroke-width:3px
    classDef rust fill:#a04b2d,stroke:#c97d62,stroke-width:1.5px,color:#ffffff
```

### Why HPMTF matters for the sulfur budget
1. **Cloud Droplet Scavenging**: $\text{HPMTF}$ is moderately soluble ($H \approx 10^4 - 10^5\text{ M atm}^{-1}$) and is rapidly scavenged by cloud droplets, bypassing traditional gas-phase $\text{SO}_2$ intermediate stages[^3].
2. **Vertical Redistribution**: In cloud-free marine boundary layers, $\text{HPMTF}$ has a longer chemical lifetime, allowing sulfur to be lofted into the free troposphere where lower temperatures favor new particle nucleation.

## Global modeling with CESM2 / CAM6-chem

In our study published in *Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics*[^4], we implemented a comprehensive DMS oxidation mechanism—incorporating explicit $\text{HPMTF}$ gas-phase photochemistry, halogen ($\text{BrO}, \text{Cl}$) reactions, and multi-phase cloud droplet uptake—into the **Community Earth System Model (CESM2 / CAM6-chem)**.

### Key atmospheric impacts

| Parameter | Classical Mechanism (No HPMTF) | Updated Explicit Mechanism (With HPMTF) | Global Shift |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Global DMS Oxidation Flux to HPMTF** | $0\text{ Tg S yr}^{-1}$ | $8.7\text{ Tg S yr}^{-1}$ | **35% of total sulfur flux** |
| **Marine Boundary Layer $\text{SO}_2$** | High ($40–120\text{ ppt}$) | Reduced by $20–45\%$ | Better agreement with ATom observations |
| **Cloud Condensation Nuclei ($\text{CCN}_{0.1\%}$)** | Overestimated in boundary layer | Redistributed to free troposphere | $-12\%$ at surface, $+18\%$ aloft |
| **Pre-Industrial Radiative Baseline** | Less reflective marine clouds | Elevated pristine background CCN | Shifts baseline albedo |
| **Anthropogenic Aerosol Forcing ($\Delta F_{\text{aer}}$)** | $-1.38\text{ W m}^{-2}$ | $-1.27\text{ W m}^{-2}$ | **$+0.11\text{ W m}^{-2}$ warming offset** |

### Interactive simulator

Explore how temperature, cloud liquid water content, and radical concentrations govern the branch point between traditional $\text{SO}_2$ formation and the $\text{HPMTF}$ autoxidation channel:

::: {.sim-card}
#### 🌊 Marine Sulfur Chemical Flux Partitioning

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof T = Inputs.range([260, 305], {value: 285, step: 1, label: "Temperature (K)"})
viewof LWC = Inputs.range([0.0, 1.0], {value: 0.20, step: 0.02, label: "Cloud liquid water content (g/m³)"})
viewof OH = Inputs.range([0.2, 5.0], {value: 1.5, step: 0.1, label: "OH radical conc. (10⁶ molec/cm³)"})

// Reaction kinetics approximation: the autoxidation H-shift is strongly
// temperature dependent (~exp(-Ea/RT)); the traditional channel tracks OH.
kAuto = 0.25 * Math.exp(0.045 * (T - 280))
kTrad = 0.35 + 0.1 * OH

hpmtfRatio = Math.min(0.75, Math.max(0.10, kAuto / (kAuto + kTrad)))
so2Ratio = 1.0 - hpmtfRatio

partition = [
  {channel: "HPMTF Channel (Autoxidation)", pct: Number((hpmtfRatio * 100).toFixed(1))},
  {channel: "Direct SO₂ / MSA Channel (Traditional)", pct: Number((so2Ratio * 100).toFixed(1))}
]

note = T < 273
  ? "❄️ Polar / Sub-polar Regime: Slower isomerization suppresses HPMTF autoxidation; traditional OH-addition dominates, prolonging DMS lifetime."
  : LWC > 0.4
  ? "☁️ Cloudy Marine Boundary Layer: High liquid water content rapidly scavenges HPMTF into cloud droplets, bypassing gas-phase SO₂ and directly feeding aqueous sulfate."
  : "☀️ Pristine Tropical / Subtropical Marine Air: Fast H-shift autoxidation routes over 40% of DMS through HPMTF, enabling sulfur lofting to the upper troposphere."

card = (label, value, colour) => html`<div class="sim-readout">
  <div class="sim-readout-label">${label}</div>
  <div class="sim-readout-value" style="color:${colour}">${value}</div>
</div>`

html`<div class="sim-readouts">
  ${card("Temperature", T + " K (" + (T - 273.15).toFixed(1) + "°C)", "#cbd5e1")}
  ${card("HPMTF Channel (Autoxidation)", partition[0].pct.toFixed(1) + "%", "#f59e0b")}
  ${card("Direct SO₂ / MSA Channel", partition[1].pct.toFixed(1) + "%", "#38bdf8")}
</div>`

Plot.plot({
  height: 150,
  marginLeft: 10,
  marginRight: 60,
  style: {background: "transparent", color: "#cbd5e1"},
  x: {domain: [0, 100], label: "share of DMS sulfur flux (%)", grid: true},
  y: {label: null, axis: null},
  color: {legend: true,
          domain: partition.map(d => d.channel),
          range: ["#f59e0b", "#38bdf8"]},

    Plot.barX(partition, {y: "channel", x: "pct", fill: "channel"}),
    Plot.text(partition, {y: "channel", x: "pct", text: d => d.pct.toFixed(1) + "%", dx: 24, fill: "#cbd5e1"})
  ]
})

html`<div style="font-size: 0.9em; background: rgba(56, 189, 248, 0.1); border-left: 4px solid #38bdf8; padding: 10px; border-radius: 4px;">${note}</div>`
```

### Climate implications and the radiative baseline

Why does a chemical intermediate matter so much for global climate projections?

The answer lies in the **pre-industrial aerosol baseline**[^5]. Anthropogenic aerosol radiative forcing is calculated as the *difference* in cloud albedo between the modern polluted atmosphere and the pre-industrial unperturbed atmosphere:

$$\Delta F_{\text{aer}} = F_{\text{modern}} - F_{\text{pre-industrial}}$$

In pre-industrial times, natural $\text{DMS}$ was the dominant source of cloud-forming particles over the oceans. Because cloud albedo is a logarithmic function of droplet concentration ($A \propto \ln N_d$), brightening clouds in an already pristine regime produces a much larger radiative response than adding aerosols to a polluted continent.

By correctly accounting for $\text{HPMTF}$ multi-phase loss and sulfur redistribution, global models refine the pre-industrial CCN baseline, reducing climate sensitivity uncertainty in IPCC-class Earth system models.

### Data and code availability

- **Model Integration**: The chemical mechanism is implemented in the Community Earth System Model (CESM2.1 / CAM6-chem), available through the [NCAR CESM repository](https://www.cesm.ucar.edu).
- **Observational Datasets**: Airborne observational validation data were obtained from the NASA Atmospheric Tomography (ATom) mission[^6].
- **Source Code**: Analysis scripts and mechanism definitions are archived on GitHub: [`kamingfung/DMS-HPMTF-CESM`](https://github.com/kamingfung).

## Key takeaways

- DMS from phytoplankton is the main natural source of sulfate CCN over the oceans; the CLAW hypothesis links it to marine cloud brightness and surface cooling.
- Classical mechanisms sent all DMS through H-abstraction and OH-addition to $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{DMSO}$; the fast intramolecular H-shift to $\text{HPMTF}$ was missing.
- In CESM2 / CAM6-chem the HPMTF route carries about $35\%$ of the DMS sulfur flux ($8.7\text{ Tg S yr}^{-1}$), cuts marine boundary layer $\text{SO}_2$ by $20$ to $45\%$ and moves CCN from the surface into the free troposphere.
- HPMTF's fate depends on clouds: in cloudy air it is scavenged into droplets as aqueous sulfate; in cloud-free air it lives long enough to loft sulfur aloft.
- Because cloud albedo goes as $\ln N_d$, changing the pristine pre-industrial baseline changes the anthropogenic forcing estimate: $\Delta F_{\text{aer}}$ moves from $-1.38$ to $-1.27\text{ W m}^{-2}$, a $+0.11\text{ W m}^{-2}$ offset.
